research.domain: LLM inference engines (local-first, for RTX 5090 / Blackwell sm_120 / Windows 11 / 32 GB VRAM + 64 GB RAM)
research.notes:
DECISIVE AXIS for this rig: Windows-native Blackwell support, not raw throughput. Most of the "fast" datacenter engines (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, LMDeploy, Aphrodite) are Linux-first and on Windows mean WSL2 — and WSL2 on Blackwell consumer cards still carries a known WDDM-paravirtualization hang bug (NVIDIA posted a $1,000 bounty; WSL2 2.7.0 + recent driver largely fixes it but it is not zero-config). For a single-human studio that wants to run a model, train a LoRA, and get back to the game, the install/maintenance tax of WSL2 + nightly cu128 wheels is the real cost, not tokens/sec. INSTALL THESE THREE for this lane:
1. Ollama (or LM Studio) — the everyday driver. Native Windows installer, day-1 RTX 5090 support since v0.5.11, zero CUDA fiddling, OpenAI-compatible server for local-LLM delegation (ollama-intern, crew agents). This is your "it just works" baseline.
2. llama.cpp (the engine under both) — install directly when you need partial GPU offload to spill a 40-50 GB GGUF across 32 GB VRAM + 64 GB RAM (-ngl + --n-cpu-moe), latest quants, or the server's full knob set. CRITICAL Blackwell gotcha: build/run with the CUDA 12.8 toolchain (-DGGML_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120). CUDA 13.x MMQ kernels segfault on sm_120 today, and the custom MMQ path can throw "invalid resource handle" — CUDA 12.8 + MMQ is the blessed combo and is ~5x faster than the wrong toolkit. Official Windows CUDA prebuilts are now 13.1-based, so a from-source 12.8 build or a community cu128 wheel is the safe path.
3. ExLlamaV3 — the performance-per-VRAM play for pure-GPU models that fit in 32 GB. EXL3 quantization (QTIP-derived) gives the best quality-at-low-bpw on NVIDIA, it actively ships Windows win_amd64 cu128 wheels (v0.0.39, May 31 2026), and it's MIT/dual. Reach for it to squeeze a 32B/70B at high quality onto the card. Note ExLlamaV2 is now ARCHIVED — use V3. WILDCARD worth installing if you run giant MoE: KTransformers. Native Windows, Apache-2.0, purpose-built CPU/GPU heterogeneous MoE — keeps hot experts on the 5090 and cold experts on the 64 GB of RAM (AMX kernels, expert-deferral), letting 100B+/DeepSeek-class MoE run on one 32 GB card at ~20 tok/s decode. This is the engine that turns your 64 GB of system RAM into a real capability rather than swap. WHAT CHANGED that inverts old advice: (a) Blackwell is no longer bleeding-edge — Ollama/LM Studio/llama.cpp/ExLlamaV3 all run sm_120 on Windows TODAY, so "wait for support" is stale. (b) The CUDA-toolkit version is now the #1 footgun: 13.x looks newer but breaks MMQ on sm_120; 12.8 is correct. (c) ExLlamaV2 → ExLlamaV3 is a hard migration (V2 archived). (d) HF TGI is effectively dead for new local work — repo archived March 2026 and relicensed off Apache (HFOIL) at v1.0; do not build on it. (e) Native-Windows vLLM still does not exist (Linux/WSL2 only) despite being the throughput king — that gap is what keeps llama.cpp/Ollama as the studio default.

On Blackwell, CUDA 12.8 + MMQ benchmarks ~pp=5611 / tg=211 on a 5090-class card; the wrong CUDA toolkit (13.x) costs up to 5x. engines.summary: The foundational local LLM runtime and the engine inside Ollama, LM Studio, llamafile and most consumer tools. Loads GGUF and is the canonical home of the GGUF quant zoo (Q4_K_M, IQ-quants, MXFP4). Best reached for when you need partial GPU offload — its -ngl (layers on GPU) plus --n-cpu-moe / -ot (keep MoE experts in RAM) lets a 40-50 GB model spill across 32 GB VRAM + 64 GB system RAM, which is exactly this rig's >32 GB use case. Blackwell gotcha is load-bearing: build/run with the CUDA 12.8 toolchain (-DGGML_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120); CUDA 13.x MMQ kernels segfault on sm_120 and the custom MMQ path can throw 'invalid resource handle' (cuBLAS is the stable fallback). Official Windows CUDA prebuilts moved to 13.1, so a from-source 12.8 build or a community cu128 wheel is the correct install today. Key knobs: -ngl, --n-cpu-moe / -ot, --flash-attn, -ctk/-ctv (KV cache quant), -ts (multi-GPU split).

Multi-GPU is automatic layer-split. Windows + Blackwell is genuinely zero-config here, which is its whole value proposition.

engines.summary: The performance-per-VRAM specialist for pure-GPU inference on NVIDIA. Its EXL3 quantization (a streamlined QTIP variant from Cornell RelaxML) delivers the best quality at low bit-rates of any mainstream NVIDIA path — EXL3 ~1.6 bpw fits a 70B on a single consumer card, and high-bpw EXL3 lets a 32B run at near-FP16 quality inside 32 GB. Crucially for this rig it actively ships Windows win_amd64 cu128 (CUDA 12.8) wheels for the RTX 5090 (v0.0.39, May 31 2026, PyTorch 2.10), so it's one of the few high-performance non-llama.cpp engines that installs cleanly on native Windows. Reach for it when a model fits in 32 GB and you want max tokens/sec + max quality from that VRAM, or to run a quantized 70B that GGUF would force partly into RAM. It is GPU-resident (no first-class CPU/RAM offload), so for >32 GB models prefer llama.cpp/KTransformers. NOTE: ExLlamaV2 is ARCHIVED (last v0.3.2, Jul 2025, MIT) — migrate to V3.

engines.summary: The engine that makes this rig's 64 GB of system RAM a real capability rather than swap. KTransformers does CPU/GPU heterogeneous MoE inference: hot/active experts stay on the 5090, cold experts live in system RAM with AMX-specialized CPU kernels, async CPU-GPU scheduling, and an 'Expert Deferral' mechanism that pushes CPU utilization toward 100%. This lets 100B+/DeepSeek-V3-class MoE models run on one 32 GB card at ~20+ tok/s decode — far beyond what fits in VRAM alone. It is Apache-2.0 and (per the repo) supports native Windows, which is rare for a research-grade hybrid engine, though Windows is less battle-tested than Linux and you should expect a more involved build (Visual Studio toolchain, CUDA 12.8). Reach for it specifically when you want to run a giant MoE locally; for dense models that fit in VRAM, ExLlamaV3/llama.cpp are simpler and faster. NUMA-aware placement and 3-layer GPU-CPU-disk prefix-cache reuse are its advanced knobs. Situational, not everyday — but uniquely valuable for the >32 GB MoE case.

engines.speed_note: Throughput king for concurrent serving (PagedAttention + continuous batching). Blackwell support is strong on Linux: v0.17+ added SM120 FP8 GEMM, v0.22 adds FlashInfer MoE + FP4 GEMM for SM120/121. But on Windows it is WSL2-only, and consumer Blackwell + WSL2 carried a WDDM hang bug.
engines.summary: The datacenter throughput champion — PagedAttention, continuous batching, tensor+pipeline parallelism — and on Linux it has first-class Blackwell support (dedicated SM120 FP8/FP4 GEMM kernels, FlashInfer paths in v0.22). The problem for THIS rig is Windows: vLLM has no native Windows build and runs only under WSL2, and consumer Blackwell cards (5090) hit a known WDDM-paravirtualization hang bug under WSL2 (NVIDIA $1,000 bounty; WSL2 2.7.0 + recent driver largely fixes graph capture but it is not zero-config). It also wants torch 2.9.0/cu128 and a CUDA-12.8 nvcc to compile for sm_120. blackwell_ready=false is scored for the native-Windows reality, not the silicon — on Linux/WSL2 it works. Reach for it only if you stand up a WSL2 (or dockerized-Linux) serving instance for many concurrent local agents; for a single human + a handful of crew calls it is overkill and a maintenance tax versus Ollama/llama.cpp. CPU/RAM offload exists (--cpu-offload-gb) but is slow and not its strength.

engines.summary: A high-throughput serving framework whose standout feature is RadixAttention — automatic KV-cache prefix reuse across requests — making it excellent for structured generation (its own SGLang DSL, JSON/grammar-constrained decoding) and multi-turn/agentic workloads. It officially lists the RTX 5090 among supported GPUs and ships FP8/NVFP4 Blackwell paths (NVIDIA NGC releases through 26.04). Same rig caveat as vLLM: no native Windows — it is Linux/WSL2 only, so blackwell_ready is scored false for this Windows box even though the silicon is supported on Linux. Reach for it over vLLM when your local serving is dominated by shared prefixes (system prompts, RAG context, agent scaffolds) and structured outputs — RadixAttention can be a large win there. For a single-human studio it is datacenter-grade tooling; only justified if you run a persistent WSL2/Linux serving node. Apache-2.0.

It keeps PagedAttention/continuous-batching throughput while broadening quant support (GGUF, EXL2, GPTQ, AWQ, FP8, NVFP4) and adding KoboldAI API compatibility, context parallelism, and the richest sampling controls in the lane. For a game studio doing character dialogue / creative generation with per-character LoRAs, that feature set is genuinely interesting (studio_fit nudged to 3). Two caveats dominate: (1) it is AGPL-3.0 — fine for internal/local use but a real constraint if you ever expose it as a network service in a product; (2) like its vLLM parent it is Linux/WSL2 only, so blackwell_ready=false for native Windows. Reach for it only inside a WSL2/Linux setup when its samplers + per-request LoRA hot-swap specifically pay off; otherwise stay on native-Windows engines.

extras.name: llama.cpp Blackwell (sm_120) Windows build — the CUDA-12.8 rule
extras.note: Build/run with the CUDA 12.8 toolkit, NOT 13.x. CMake: cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 -DGGML_CUDA_FORCE_MMQ=ON; then cmake --build build --config Release -j. CUDA 13.x MMQ kernels segfault on sm_120 and MXFP4 fails to compile ('mma with block scale' unsupported); the custom MMQ path can throw 'invalid resource handle' — if so, fall back to cuBLAS (stable on 5090). Correct combo (12.8 + MMQ) benched ~pp=5611 / tg=211 vs up to 5x slower with the wrong toolkit. Official Windows prebuilts are now CUDA-13.1, so either build from source with 12.8 or grab a community cu128 wheel.

extras.name: llama.cpp >32 GB partial offload on 32 GB VRAM + 64 GB RAM
extras.note: For a model larger than VRAM: dense models use -ngl <N> to put as many layers on GPU as fit, rest spill to RAM. For MoE (DeepSeek/Qwen-MoE/Mixtral) keep experts in RAM and attention on GPU: -ngl 99 with --n-cpu-moe <N> (newer flag) or -ot 'blk\.\d+\.ffn_.*_exps.=CPU' to pin expert tensors to CPU. Add --flash-attn and quantize the KV cache (-ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0) to fit more context. Tune --threads to physical P-cores of the Core Ultra 9. This is how a ~40-50 GB GGUF runs usefully on this box.

extras.name: ik_llama.cpp hybrid big-MoE tuning (Windows, Blackwell)
extras.note: Build with -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 (CUDA 12.8). Use -ngl 99 plus -ot expert-placement regex to keep routed experts in RAM and dense/attention on the 5090. AVOID -rtr unless you understand it. GPU-offload prompt-processing threshold differs from mainline (~32 * total_experts/active_experts tokens). Try its SOTA quants (IQ-K, Trellis) for better quality-per-GB. Benchmark against mainline llama.cpp on your exact model — ik wins on many big-MoE configs but has documented regressions on some.

extras.name: ExLlamaV3 on Windows + RTX 5090 (cu128 wheel)
extras.note: Install the prebuilt win_amd64 cu128 wheel matching your Python (cp310-cp314) + PyTorch 2.10 from the v0.0.39 release — no source build needed on Blackwell. Quantize an HF model to EXL3 at a target bpw that fits 32 GB (e.g. ~4-5 bpw for a 32B near-FP16; ~2.x bpw to fit a 70B). Use tensor-parallel mode only if you add a second GPU. This is the highest quality-per-VRAM pure-GPU path on this rig and needs no WSL2.

extras.name: KTransformers giant-MoE on one 5090 + 64 GB RAM
extras.note: Use KTransformers to run a 100B+/DeepSeek-class MoE that cannot fit in 32 GB VRAM: it keeps hot/active experts on the GPU and cold experts in system RAM with AMX CPU kernels + expert-deferral, reaching ~20+ tok/s decode on a single 5090. Set --kt-num-gpu-experts to the count of experts you want resident on the 5090 (raise until VRAM ~full), enable NUMA-aware placement, and use FP8/BF16 per-channel precision. Native Windows is supported but expect a Visual Studio + CUDA 12.8 build; budget setup time. Best home for frontier open MoE weights on this box.

extras.name: vLLM on RTX 5090 via WSL2 (if you need a throughput node)
extras.note: Native Windows is unsupported — run under WSL2. Upgrade WSL2 to >=2.7.0 (fixes Blackwell dxgkrnl/CUDA-graph-capture hang) and a recent NVIDIA driver. Install torch 2.9.0+cu128 and vLLM v0.17+ (v0.22 for best SM120 FP8/FP4). Launch with --dtype fp8 on the 5090 for the dedicated SM120 FP8 GEMM. Use --cpu-offload-gb only as a last resort (slow). Only worth it for many concurrent local agents; for single-user work prefer Ollama/llama.cpp.

extras.name: Unsloth (Blackwell / RTX 50-series LoRA + QLoRA fine-tuning)
extras.note: Adjacent training tool, directly relevant to the studio's LoRA/style fine-tuning workload. Officially documents RTX 50-series/Blackwell support with cu128; 2x-faster, lower-VRAM QLoRA fits 8B-14B (and quantized larger) training on a single 32 GB 5090. The training-side counterpart to these inference engines on this exact rig (note: Linux/WSL2 is the smoother path for training).

extras.note: Cross-engine 2026 comparison (vLLM / Ollama / LM Studio / llama.cpp and others) useful for sanity-checking throughput-vs-latency-vs-VRAM positioning when picking an engine per task.

verify.receipt: Verified all 14 claimed engines against live GitHub releases pages, official documentation, and web searches conducted 2026-06-02. Major findings: Ollama's version is wrong by a wide margin (v0.6.2 claimed vs v0.30.0 live); Aphrodite Engine is six major versions behind (v0.10.0 claimed vs v0.21.0 live) and its repo has moved to dphnAI/; LMDeploy has a version error (0.12.3 vs 0.13.0) and its Blackwell status is inverted (false claimed, but v0.13.0 explicitly adds Blackwell support); vLLM's Blackwell status is also inverted (false claimed, but confirmed working from v0.17.0 onward with sm_120 FP8 GEMM); llamafile is two patch versions behind (0.10.0 vs 0.10.3); LM Studio is two minor versions behind (0.4.13 vs 0.4.15). MLC-LLM's v0.19.0 version claim cannot be confirmed from any live source — only a v0.1.dev0 pre-release tag is visible on GitHub — making it the most suspect entry. TGI's license shows as Apache-2.0 on the archived main branch, contradicting the HFOIL claim that was historically correct for shipped v1.0+ releases; flagged as requiring direct compliance verification. Three engines are marked blackwell_ready: true without supporting documentation: ExLlamaV3, ik_llama.cpp, and llamafile — none of these repos mention sm_120 or Blackwell explicitly. Three notable omissions identified: mistral.rs (Rust-native, production-quality, widely deployed), NVIDIA Triton Inference Server (the standard production serving layer for the engines listed), and Apple MLX/mlx-lm (the dominant Apple Silicon inference path).

As of 2026 WSL2 2.7.0 finally makes vLLM CUDA-graph capture work on Blackwell sm_120 (~140 tok/s Qwen3-14B-AWQ vs ~17 eager, source: vllm#37242), so WSL2 is now usable — but it is still a Linux VM, not native. Triton specifically DEPRECATED Windows (last build 2.51.0 / 25.01) — do not pick it for this box. INSTALL THESE THREE for this lane: (1) **llama-swap** (MIT, v222, true native-Windows Go binary) as the front-door router/hot-swapper — it owns the "one OpenAI endpoint, many models, load-on-demand, unload-on-idle" problem on 32 GB VRAM and speaks llama.cpp + vLLM + TabbyAPI + embeddings/rerank + sd.cpp. This is the one engine that is BOTH native-Windows AND solves the actual single-workstation multi-model problem. (2) **llama.cpp llama-server** as the native-Windows upstream that llama-swap drives for GGUF + partial CPU/RAM offload (the 64 GB RAM lets ~40-50 GB models spill past 32 GB VRAM) — it is the realistic heavy-LLM path on Windows without WSL2. (3) **LiteLLM proxy** (MIT core) ONLY IF the studio needs to blend local endpoints with hosted APIs (Claude/OpenAI) behind one key with budgets/fallback — it is a routing/governance layer, NOT an inference engine, and adds nothing if everything is local. SECOND TIER, WSL2 only: stand up **vLLM** (Apache-2.0, v0.22.0, sm_120 kernels shipped) or **SGLang** (Apache-2.0, v0.5.12, RadixAttention prefix-cache) inside WSL2 when you need real continuous/in-flight batching for a fleet of concurrent LLM-crew agents hitting one model — that is where paged-KV + prefix caching beats llama.cpp by a wide margin. Point llama-swap at the WSL2 vLLM port so the native router still fronts it. For embeddings/rerank specifically, run **Text Embeddings Inference (TEI)** (Apache-2.0, v1.9.3, sm_120 experimental) in Docker/WSL2 — it is the fast, Blackwell-aware embed/rerank server; Infinity is the cross-platform alternative but its last release was Aug 2025 (slowing). AVOID for this rig: Triton (Windows deprecated), KServe (needs a Kubernetes cluster — pure datacenter), Ray Serve (multi-node Python orchestration, overkill for one box; only reach for it if you genuinely run an embedding+rerank+LLM graph with queue-depth autoscaling), OpenLLM/BentoML (BentoML core is healthy but the local-serve value is just a vLLM wrapper; build it only when packaging a Bento for cloud deploy). TorchServe is effectively dead — Meta/AWS marked it no-longer-actively-maintained, no security patches; do not adopt. WHAT CHANGED: the old "use Triton/Ray for serious serving" advice is wrong on a Windows workstation in 2026 — the native winner is llama-swap-over-llama.cpp, with WSL2 vLLM/SGLang as the batching escalation and TEI as the embed/rerank sidecar.

engines.speed_note: Zero inference overhead — it is a thin Go proxy. Cost is the model swap latency (unload current upstream, spawn new one, load weights); mitigated by keeping hot models resident via `ttl` and grouping models that fit together. engines.summary: A single-binary Go reverse proxy that puts ONE OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible endpoint in front of many local inference servers and hot-swaps the upstream based on the requested `model` field — load-on-demand, unload-on-idle. This is the one engine in this lane that is BOTH genuinely native-Windows (prebuilt binary + WinGet, with explicit Windows shutdown/nvidia-smi fixes in v217/v222) AND solves the real single-workstation problem: 32 GB VRAM can't hold many models at once, so you swap. Config is one YAML file mapping model names to launch commands; key knobs are `ttl` (seconds before an idle model unloads to free VRAM), `cmd`/`cmdStop` per model, and `groups` to keep a set of small models co-resident. Speaks llama.cpp's full surface including `/v1/embeddings` and `/v1/rerank|/v1/reranking|/rerank`, plus stable-diffusion.cpp and whisper.cpp endpoints, so it can front your whole local stack. Blackwell-ready because it runs nothing itself — it just launches a Blackwell-capable upstream (native llama-server, or a WSL2 vLLM). No batching/observability beyond what the upstream provides; pair with llama.cpp for native-Windows heavy lifting.

research.domain: Quantization frameworks & formats — algorithms, tools, and weight formats for shrinking models to fit VRAM and/or accelerate inference (GGUF, GPTQ, AWQ, EXL2/EXL3, bitsandbytes NF4/INT8, FP8, NVFP4/MXFP4, HQQ, AutoRound, llm-compressor)
research.notes:
DECISIVE AXIS for this rig: format-to-engine compatibility ON WINDOWS, weighted by quality-per-bit at the sizes a 32 GB-VRAM card runs. Quantization is not one tool — it is a producer/consumer split: a QUANTIZER (llm-compressor, GPTQModel, AutoRound, HQQ, llama-quantize, exllamav3 convert) emits a FORMAT (GGUF, GPTQ, AWQ, EXL3, FP8, NVFP4) that a specific INFERENCE ENGINE consumes. The KB's job is to map who-makes-what and who-runs-what on this exact box. WHAT TO INSTALL (this rig, this lane), in priority order:
1) llama.cpp + GGUF (k-quants/i-quants, imatrix). The only first-class native-Windows story. MIT, runs on sm_120 today (build with CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 against CUDA 12.8 to skip PTX JIT — the #1 perf trap), and the 64 GB system RAM makes partial GPU offload (-ngl + --n-cpu-moe) viable for models a hair over 32 GB. This is the studio's default inference + quantize stack. Daily-driver quant: Q4_K_M (or IQ4_XS with an imatrix for tighter VRAM); Q5_K_M/Q6_K when a model fully fits 32 GB and quality matters.
2) ExLlamaV3 (EXL3) for the single-GPU quality-per-bit ceiling. v0.0.39, MIT, prebuilt Windows wheels + triton-windows. QTIP/Viterbi-coded — EXL3 at ~3.5–4.0 bpw is the best perplexity-per-byte on one 5090, and the fused KV-cache quant lets a 32B sit comfortably in 32 GB with long context. Serve via TabbyAPI (OpenAI-compatible). This is the "I have one great GPU and want maximum smart-per-VRAM" path.
3) GGUF-via-frontend (LM Studio / KoboldCpp / Ollama) as the zero-friction local-delegation layer for the LLM crew — all wrap the same llama.cpp/GGUF stack, all run native on Windows. THE FP4 INVERSION (what changed, and the honest caveat): NVFP4/MXFP4 are Blackwell-native tensor-core 4-bit formats — on paper the headline win of owning a 5090 (≈1.6× over BF16, hardware-accelerated only on sm_120+). But on native Windows in mid-2026 the consumer story is still immature: the production NVFP4 path (TensorRT-LLM + ModelOpt) on a GeForce 5090 is WSL2-only and community-patched; in llama.cpp the NVFP4 core kernels merged (PRs #20644/#21074/#21227/#21455/#21539) but the Blackwell-native acceleration dispatch (PR #22196) was still open at writing, so a stock master build collects memory savings without full tensor-core speedup, and NVFP4-vs-Q4_K_M quality has no settled independent benchmark yet. CONCLUSION: treat FP4 as a high-upside experimental lane to watch, not the production default — Q4_K_M/EXL3 still win for reliability on Windows today. Re-evaluate once #22196 lands in mainline. TRAINING/LoRA note (real studio workload): bitsandbytes NF4 is still the standard QLoRA weight type, but its CUDA kernels remain shaky on sm_120 (community reports of sm_120 incompatibility and a small-model energy paradox where 4-bit is ~58% of FP16 throughput on the 5090), so expect to build from source / use nightly multi-backend wheels and verify per-version. For style/character LoRA on this rig, NF4 QLoRA works but is not the smooth path it is on Ampere/Hopper — budget setup time. DATACENTER tools catalogued for completeness but scored down for a single workstation: llm-compressor (the FP8/NVFP4/INT4 PRODUCER for vLLM — Apache, v0.11.0, but its consumer vLLM is Linux-first/WSL2 on Windows) and TensorRT-LLM (max NVFP4 throughput, WSL2-only on GeForce). Both are useful if the studio ever stands up a Linux box; on this Windows-only rig they are quantizer-of-record-for-when-you-need-FP8, not daily drivers.

engines.summary: The library behind QLoRA — NF4 (4-bit NormalFloat) and LLM.int8() — used to fine-tune and load HF models in low precision via Transformers/PEFT. For this studio it matters mainly as the LoRA/style fine-tuning weight type, the real local-training workload: NF4 QLoRA lets you train adapters on models that wouldn't otherwise fit. The honest Blackwell story is the catch: bitsandbytes kernels were reported incompatible with sm_120, and on the 5090 NF4 shows a throughput/energy paradox on small models (4-bit ~58% of FP16 t/s; on sub-1.5B models it can burn MORE energy per token than FP16). Official Windows wheels exist and the multi-backend refactor adds CUDA 13.0, but pinning a build that cleanly supports sm_120 may require nightly/continuous-release wheels or a source build — verify per version. Knobs: bnb_4bit_quant_type=nf4, double-quant, bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=bfloat16. Note it does NOT produce NVFP4 — NF4 is a distinct 4-bit scheme, not Blackwell's hardware FP4.

extras.name: Build llama.cpp native for RTX 5090 (sm_120) on Windows — avoid the 5x PTX-JIT trap
extras.note: Install CUDA Toolkit 12.8+ (cu128). Configure: `cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=120 -DGGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON`. Build: `cmake --build build --config Release -j`. Setting arch=120 bakes sm_120 SASS so end users skip PTX JIT (~5x faster cold start). cu128 ships Blackwell-tuned cuBLAS. Verify the GPU is detected with `llama-cli --version` / `-ngl 99` and watch for 'CUDA0' device line.

extras.name: llama.cpp launch tuned for 32 GB VRAM + 64 GB RAM (full-fit and partial-offload)
extras.note: Full fit (model <~30 GB at chosen quant): `llama-server -m model.Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 --no-mmap -c 16384 -fa --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080`. --no-mmap forces weights into VRAM (prevents Blackwell illegal-memory-access/OOM at long context). Partial offload for a model a bit over 32 GB: drop -ngl to fit (e.g. -ngl 60) OR for MoE use `--n-cpu-moe N` to keep N expert layers on the 64 GB RAM + Core Ultra 9. -fa enables flash attention. Add KV-cache quant `--cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0` to stretch context.

extras.name: Quantize an HF model to GGUF with an imatrix (best low-bit quality)
extras.note: 1) Convert: `python convert_hf_to_gguf.py <hf-dir> --outfile model-f16.gguf --outtype f16`. 2) Build imatrix on a calibration corpus (e.g. wiki.train / groups-merged.txt): `llama-imatrix -m model-f16.gguf -f calib.txt -o model.imatrix -ngl 99`. 3) Quantize with the imatrix for i-quants: `llama-quantize --imatrix model.imatrix model-f16.gguf model-IQ4_XS.gguf IQ4_XS`. Daily driver without imatrix: `llama-quantize model-f16.gguf model-Q4_K_M.gguf Q4_K_M`. Quality ladder for 32 GB: Q6_K/Q5_K_M (when it fits) > Q4_K_M > IQ4_XS(+imatrix) > IQ3_M.

extras.name: ExLlamaV3 / EXL3 on Windows + TabbyAPI serving
extras.note: Install: `pip install exllamav3` then `pip install triton-windows` (Triton is required on Windows; the repo ships prebuilt CUDA wheels for cu124+). Quantize: `python -m exllamav3.convert -i <hf-model> -o <out-exl3> -b 4.0` (target bpw; 3.5–4.0 ~ BF16 quality, ~2.5–3.0 for tight fits). Serve via TabbyAPI (OpenAI-compatible) — set the model dir, enable quantized KV-cache (`cache_mode: Q6`/`Q4`) to free VRAM for long context on the 5090. EXL3 only — it will not load GGUF/GPTQ.

extras.name: NVFP4 on RTX 5090 — the realistic 2026 Windows paths
extras.note: Native-Windows production NVFP4 is NOT turnkey. Options: (a) ComfyUI/diffusion — install latest ComfyUI with cu128 + a Blackwell PyTorch build; NVFP4 Flux/Wan checkpoints load but expect occasional failures (track ComfyUI issues). (b) LLM serving — run TensorRT-LLM under WSL2 (NVIDIA documents GeForce RTX 50 NVFP4 via WSL); 30B-class MoE in NVFP4 on a 32 GB 5090 currently needs the community C++ runtime patches (trtllm-nvfp4-blackwell-fix). (c) llama.cpp — NVFP4 GGUFs run on a recent master for the memory savings, but the Blackwell tensor-core accel (PR #22196) was still open at writing, so don't expect full FP4 speedup yet. Verdict: prototype only; keep Q4_K_M/EXL3 as production.

extras.name: Produce GPTQ/AWQ checkpoints with GPTQModel (AutoGPTQ/AutoAWQ are archived)
extras.note: Install: `pip install gptqmodel`. AutoGPTQ (Apr 2025) and AutoAWQ (May 2025) are both archived — GPTQModel is the maintained producer. Quantize GPTQ: load model with `GPTQModel.load(...)`, pass a calibration dataset and `QuantizeConfig(bits=4, group_size=128, format='gptq')`, then `.quantize(calib)` and `.save(out)`. For AWQ set the AWQ method/format. Output runs in vLLM via Marlin/Machete kernels (Linux/WSL2 on this rig) or locally via Transformers. For single-GPU local use, EXL3 usually beats GPTQ on quality-per-bit.

extras.name: Calibration-free quick-shrink with HQQ
extras.note: When you have no calibration corpus or need a model shrunk NOW: `from transformers import HqqConfig; cfg = HqqConfig(nbits=4, group_size=64)` then load the model with `quantization_config=cfg`. No dataset, minutes not hours. For inference speed attach a fast backend (torchao/Marlin) where supported. Good for vision models too.

extras.name: TabbyAPI (OpenAI-compatible server for ExLlamaV2/V3)
extras.note: The standard front-end to serve EXL3 (and EXL2) models with an OpenAI-compatible API on Windows — pair with ExLlamaV3 for the max-quality-per-VRAM local endpoint feeding the LLM crew.

extras.name: LM Studio / KoboldCpp / Ollama (GGUF frontends)
extras.note: All three wrap the llama.cpp/GGUF stack with native Windows installers and OpenAI-compatible endpoints — the zero-friction local-delegation layer for the crew. research.domain: Attention backends & GPU kernel libraries (tensor/inference/training engine acceleration layer)
research.notes: DECISIVE AXIS for this rig: the RTX 5090 is "desktop Blackwell" (sm_120 / GB202), which is a DIFFERENT chip from datacenter Blackwell (sm_100 B200 / sm_103 B300). sm_120 uses the old HMMA register-to-register MMA family and PHYSICALLY LACKS the TMEM tensor-memory subsystem (UTCHMMA/UTMALDG instructions) that the warp-specialized FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4 kernels are built on. Consequence that inverts naive advice: the newest FlashAttention (FA4 v4.0.0.beta4, Mar 2026) and FA3 DO NOT and CANNOT run on the RTX 5090 — "no amount of software patching can fix it" (solatticus gist; sglang #10564). On sm_120 you fall back to FlashAttention-2-class kernels. The real winners for THIS rig, in order: 1) INSTALL cuDNN SDPA (it's already in your PyTorch). On the 5090 the cuDNN fused-attention backend is the single FASTEST attention kernel measured — ~203.6 TFLOPS, 97.2% of speed-of-light, beating even hand-tuned CUDA FA2 (190 TFLOPS) and the official flash-attn package (gau-nernst fa-5090 benchmark). It ships by default in PyTorch >= 2.5, autograd + torch.compile aware, zero build. For LLM decode/prefill and training on this rig, torch SDPA (which picks cuDNN) is the no-brainer floor. 2) INSTALL SageAttention (2++ for now, 3 when you want FP4) — this is the diffusion/ComfyUI win and the headline reason to bother past SDPA. SageAttention2++ (v2.2.0, Apache-2.0, commercial-OK) quantizes QK to INT8 + PV to FP8 and runs 2-3x faster than FA2 on the same card with no end-to-end quality loss; SageAttention3 adds true Blackwell FP4 microscaling for ~1038 TOPS / 5x on the 5090 (NeurIPS'25 spotlight, arXiv 2505.11594). This is what makes Flux / Wan / Hunyuan / SD3.5 generation fast on this rig. Pair it with triton-windows. 3) Have FlexAttention (PyTorch built-in, BSD-3) in your back pocket for any custom mask (sliding-window, ALiBi, document/prefix-LM) — you write the mask as a Python score_mod/block_mask and torch.compile fuses it into a block-sparse FA2-class Triton kernel on sm_120. It's the "I need a weird attention pattern without writing CUDA" tool. WINDOWS REALITY / the load-bearing pitfall: never `pip install xformers` into ComfyUI's embedded Python on this rig. xformers (a) has no sm_120 wheel and refuses (capability 12.0 "too new"), and (b) drags its own torch pin that SILENTLY force-downgrades your cu128/cu130 nightly back to a stable CPU/older-CUDA build — the single biggest hidden trap on Windows Blackwell (ComfyUI #6980, AUTOMATIC1111 #16818). The modern Windows-native stack is: PyTorch cu128 (or cu130 nightly for NVFP4) + triton-windows (MIT, sm_120 officially supported, bundles its own CUDA/TinyCC toolchain) + SageAttention + torch.compile + SDPA. triton-windows is the enabling layer for everything Triton-compiled (SageAttention, FlexAttention) on Windows without WSL2. WHAT CHANGED RECENTLY: (1) FA4 launched (Mar 2026) but is datacenter-only — do not chase it for the 5090. (2) cuDNN's frontend now exposes sm_120 fused attention and is the practical speed king on this card. (3) SageAttention3's FP4 path went public (code Sep 2025) and is the first kernel to actually exploit the 5090's FP4 tensor cores. (4) triton-windows reached 3.7.x with first-class Blackwell support, killing most "build SageAttention from source" pain. Net: for a single-workstation studio doing local LLM + ComfyUI diffusion + LoRA, you install exactly THREE things in this lane — cuDNN-backed SDPA (free), SageAttention, and triton-windows — and you skip xformers, FlashInfer, PagedAttention internals, Marlin/Machete (those are vLLM/datacenter server-side and either Linux-first or wrapped automatically by the engine).

engines.speed_note: Mixed-input quantized GEMM kernels (4-bit weights) that make GPTQ/AWQ models run fast and small — ~4x memory savings. Machete is Hopper-optimized (sm_90a); Marlin now covers Turing+; on the 5090 they accelerate quantized weights, but you get them automatically by loading a GPTQ/AWQ model in vLLM, not by installing them.
engines.summary: Two mixed-precision GEMM kernels for quantized LLM weights, both living inside vLLM: Marlin (the original 4-bit GPTQ kernel, now extended to Turing+ as of Apr 2026) and Machete (Neural Magic's Hopper-class successor for w4a16/w8a16 GPTQ + compressed-tensors, ~4x memory savings). These are the GEMM half of the speed story (attention kernels are the other half) and matter on this rig because a 32 GB-VRAM card leans hard on 4-bit quantization to fit big models. You don't install them — vLLM auto-selects Marlin/Machete when you load a GPTQ/AWQ/compressed-tensors model. For THIS rig they're situational the same way vLLM is: Linux-first, so WSL2/Docker. On the 5090 they accelerate quantized weights, though the FP4/NVFP4 GEMM path on consumer sm_120 still has reported bugs (FlashInfer/CUTLASS grouped block-scaled GEMM issues), so prefer INT4 GPTQ/AWQ over NVFP4 for now. Note this lane's GEMM kernels are about WEIGHT quantization; SageAttention is the analogous quantization win on the ATTENTION side.

engines.summary: Meta's long-standing memory-efficient attention library that powered the SD1.5/SDXL era. On THIS rig it is the canonical Blackwell trap and the reason this lane has a load-bearing warning: do NOT pip install xformers into ComfyUI's embedded Python. Two failure modes: (1) there's no official sm_120 wheel, so memory_efficient_attention_forward errors out requiring capability <= (9,0) while the 5090 reports (12,0); and (2) far worse, xformers resolves its own torch dependency and SILENTLY force-downgrades your cu128/cu130 nightly to a stable/older build, breaking the whole environment — the single biggest hidden trap on Windows Blackwell. The correct replacement on this rig is triton-windows + torch.compile + SDPA (cuDNN), with SageAttention for the speed that xformers used to provide. A community fork (xiangxin2025cn) compiles xformers 0.0.32 for sm_120 with CUTLASS 4.0, but there is no reason to take that risk when SDPA+SageAttention are faster and Windows-native. extras.name: Modern Windows-native Blackwell ComfyUI attention stack (NO xformers)
extras.note: The canonical 5090/Windows stack. (1) PyTorch cu128 stable, OR cu130 nightly if you want NVFP4 2x (cu128 NVFP4 can be slower than fp8). (2) `pip install -U "triton-windows<3.7"` (pin to your torch: 3.6 needs torch>=2.10). (3) SageAttention via Kijai precompiled wheel or DazzleML installer — NOT a from-source build. (4) In ComfyUI use KJNodes 'Patch Sage Attention' node with backend sageattn_qk_int8_pv_fp16_cuda; enable torch.compile node. NEVER `pip install xformers` into the embedded python — it silently force-downgrades torch and bricks the env. AVOID the global --use-sage-attention flag on Qwen/Wan (black output); use the patch node per-model instead.

extras.name: Verify cuDNN SDPA is the active attention backend on the 5090
extras.note: cuDNN SDPA is the fastest 5090 attention and free in PyTorch. Sanity-check it's selected: `import torch; print(torch.backends.cuda.cudnn_sdp_enabled(), torch.backends.cuda.flash_sdp_enabled())`. Force a backend with `with torch.nn.attention.sdpa_kernel(torch.nn.attention.SDPBackend.CUDNN_ATTENTION):` around your forward pass. Just call torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention and let torch pick — on sm_120 it lands on cuDNN. Requires a cu128+ torch build so the sm_120 kernels are present (stock CPU/old-CUDA wheels won't have them).

extras.name: Install community FlashAttention-2 wheels for sm_120 on Windows (only if a lib hard-requires flash_attn)
extras.note: Don't build FA from source on Windows. Use prebuilt sm_120 wheels: loscrossos/lib_flashattention v2.7.4.post1 (torch 2.7.0 / py3.12, Win+Linux), or lldacing / Zarrac / marcorez8 wheels for torch 2.8 cu128. Match torch + python + CUDA exactly to the wheel tag. In vLLM, set env VLLM_FLASH_ATTN_VERSION=2 to force the FA2 path (FA3/FA4 don't exist on sm_120). Remember cuDNN SDPA is faster anyway — only install FA2 to satisfy a hard import.

extras.name: SageAttention3 FP4 build for the 5090 (max diffusion speed)
extras.note: For the ~5x FP4 path: needs python>=3.13, torch>=2.8.0, CUDA>=12.8, triton-windows installed first. Build the sageattention3_blackwell sub-module from source (python setup.py install). API: `sageattn3_blackwell(q,k,v,is_causal=False)` on fp16/bf16 tensors shaped (B,H,S,D). FP4 is NOT guaranteed lossless on all models — use the recommended hybrid: SageAttention2++ on the first and last diffusion timesteps, SA3 FP4 in the middle, to protect output quality. For most users SA2++ (pip install sageattention==2.2.0 --no-build-isolation) is the safer default and already 2-3x over FA2.

extras.name: vLLM on the 5090 via WSL2/Docker (local OpenAI endpoint for the LLM crew)
extras.note: vLLM has no native Windows (13 orchestration-layer blockers) — run under WSL2 or the BoltzmannEntropy/vLLM-5090 or jvadura/vLLM-Blackwell Docker images. Working combo: torch 2.9.0+cu128. Use --dtype fp8 (and fp8 KV cache) to exploit the 5090's FP8 tensor cores; load GPTQ/AWQ models so Marlin/Machete GEMM kicks in for the 32 GB VRAM budget. With 64 GB system RAM you can also use --cpu-offload-gb to spill a few GB of weights to RAM for models slightly over 32 GB VRAM. Prefer INT4 GPTQ/AWQ over NVFP4 on sm_120 for now (NVFP4 grouped GEMM bugs).

extras.name: RAM-offload for >32 GB models on this 64 GB rig (llama.cpp / GGUF partial offload)
extras.note: When a model exceeds 32 GB VRAM, the 64 GB system RAM makes partial offload viable. With llama.cpp/Ollama, set --n-gpu-layers to push as many transformer layers as fit onto the 5090 and leave the rest on CPU/RAM (GGUF). This is the simplest Windows-native path (no WSL2) for big quantized LLMs; attention on the GPU layers still benefits from the engine's CUDA kernels. For MoE specifically, KTransformers-style CPU+GPU expert offload keeps hot experts on the 5090 and cold experts in RAM.

extras.name: DazzleML comfyui-triton-and-sageattention-installer
extras.note: One-click.bat that installs Python 3.13 + PyTorch nightly cu130 + triton-windows + ComfyUI + SageAttention + 28 pre-verified custom nodes for RTX 5090 on Windows in ~20 min. The fastest way to get the modern Blackwell attention stack working without fighting silent torch downgrades. Good starting point even if you later customize.

extras.name: Kijai precompiled SageAttention + Triton wheels (KJNodes)
extras.note: Kijai's precompiled sageattention/triton wheels + KJNodes 'Patch Sage Attention' node are the de-facto community standard for Blackwell ComfyUI — they sidestep the PyTorch-header patching that native SageAttention source builds require on Windows.

extras.name: gau-nernst: Writing Speed-of-Light Flash Attention for 5090 in CUDA C++
extras.note: The definitive 5090 attention benchmark + teardown. Establishes the rig's pecking order (cuDNN 203 TFLOPS > hand-tuned CUDA FA2 198 > flash-attn 190) and documents which instructions sm_120 has (cp.async, ldmatrix, mma.m16n8k16 — Ampere-class) vs lacks (no MXFP8/NVFP4 MMA in Triton). Read this to understand why the 5090 is FA2-class, not FA4-class.

extras.name: FlashAttention-4 Cannot Run on RTX 5090 (SM120) — A Deep Investigation
extras.note: The single best explanation of the decisive hardware fact in this lane: sm_120 (GB202) physically lacks the TMEM subsystem and UTCHMMA instruction family that FA3/FA4 require, uses old HMMA instead, so no FA4 on the 5090 ever. Settles the 'why can't I just install the newest FlashAttention' question definitively.

extras.name: lilting.ch — ComfyUI on Blackwell GPUs: why sm_120 fails and the PyTorch Nightly fix
extras.note: Clear writeup of why sm_120 fails on stock PyTorch and the cu128/cu130 nightly fix, plus the xformers-downgrade trap. Good companion to the ComfyUI #6980 thread for first-time Blackwell setup.

verdicts.fixes: Version description 'cuDNN 9.x / nvidia-cudnn-frontend (rolling)' is imprecise. verdicts.fixes: Version claim '2.2.0 (SageAttention2++)' is confusing: the PyPI package 'sageattention' tops at 1.0.6 (released Nov 20 2024). The '2.2.0' label refers to the GitHub release tag only, not the pip-installable package version. The 'latest_version' field should clarify that 2.2.0 is a GitHub tag and the pip version is 1.0.6. Blackwell_ready is correct for sm_120 (RTX 5090 was confirmed working at 560T throughput per Feb 2025 update). Windows support is confirmed via PR #323 (MSVC compilation support).

verdicts.fixes: Developer attribution is stale. The woct0rdho/triton-windows repo was ARCHIVED by its owner on February 18, 2026 and is now read-only. Active development has moved to the official triton-lang/triton-windows repo, maintained by woct0rdho and jammm. The PyPI package 'triton-windows' at version 3.7.0.post26 (released May 14, 2026) is still the correct install target and is current. The researcher should update developer to 'triton-lang org (woct0rdho + jammm maintainers; original woct0rdho fork archived 2026-02-18)'. MIT license and Windows-only platform confirmed correct.
verdicts.note: Version 3.7.0.post26 verified live on PyPI as of May 14 2026. Blackwell_ready claim is plausible given the package tracks upstream Triton which has Blackwell support, but no explicit confirmation found in search results for sm_120 specifically.

verdicts.fixes: The claim 'stable since PyTorch 2.5' overstates stability. FlexAttention was introduced as a PROTOTYPE feature in PyTorch 2.5, not a stable API. As of 2026, it remains in active development with known limitations in SGLang (page_size must be 1, no FP8 KV cache, no sliding window, no speculative decoding, no multimodal). X86 CPU support was added only in PyTorch 2.6. The 'current in 2.12+' claim is consistent with PyTorch 2.12.0 release evidence. Blackwell_ready is plausible since it compiles via Triton. BSD-3-Clause license for PyTorch is correct.
verdicts.note: Developer attribution should note PyTorch team broadly, not just Meta. The flex_attention.py file exists at the claimed repo URL. vLLM exposes it as --attention-backend flex_attention confirming production use.

verdicts.fixes: Latest version is 2.8.4, not the vague '2.8.x line'. The 'community sm_120 wheels at 2.7.4.post1 (loscrossos/lib_flashattention)' is plausible but unverified from live sources. FA2 is confirmed to target SM80 through SM120 (Blackwell) as the production C++/CUDA implementation. BSD-3-Clause license confirmed. Note that on Blackwell, FA2 uses Triton-based fallback paths (not the optimized TMEM paths FA4 uses on SM100/SM110).
verdicts.note: Multiple open issues confirm community Blackwell (sm_120) activity. The repo resolves correctly at github.com/Dao-AILab/flash-attention.

verdicts.fixes: Two significant errors: (1) Version '4.0.0.beta4' is WRONG — the latest release as of May 27, 2026 is fa4-v4.0.0.beta15, not beta4. (2) blackwell_ready: false is PARTIALLY WRONG for sm_120. FA4 beta6 added 'SM120 forward pass (Blackwell GeForce / DGX Spark)' and subsequent betas added SM120 backward pass and varlen support (beta7/beta8). SM120 code paths exist in FA4 as of beta15. HOWEVER, SM120 (RTX 5090) lacks the TMEM subsystem that FA4's primary fast path on SM100/SM110 relies on; the SM120 path uses SM80-style register MMA ('FlashAttentionForwardSm120, 4 warps, SM80 MMA + SM120 SMEM capacity'). The blackwell_ready flag should reflect that sm_120 has a functional but non-TMEM-optimized code path in FA4 beta15. The platform claim 'linux' only is confirmed correct — FA4 is Linux-only.
verdicts.note: FA4 is officially described as targeting 'Hopper and Blackwell (e.g. H100, B200)' — the datacenter framing is accurate for the primary optimized path. The earlier gist (solatticus) documented the TMEM limitation but predates beta6's sm_120 forward pass addition. State as of beta15: sm_120 has functional (non-TMEM) paths, not the full FA4 feature set.

verdicts.fixes: Version 0.6.12 confirmed on PyPI (released May 29, 2026). blackwell_ready: true is OVERSTATED for consumer sm_120 (RTX 5090, RTX PRO 6000). The precompiled cubin wheels in flashinfer-cubin 0.6.11/0.6.12 ship zero sm_120/sm_121 cubins — all AOT-compiled cubins target sm_100a, sm_100f, sm_103a (datacenter Blackwell). Consumer Blackwell sm_120 falls through to wrong-arch cubins and produces degenerate output for NVFP4/FP4 operations. FlashInfer is properly blackwell_ready for sm_100/sm_103 datacenter GPUs (B200, DGX), but NOT for sm_120 consumer Blackwell as of 0.6.12. Platform 'linux' only is confirmed correct. Developer attribution should note this is not directly NVIDIA-backed in the corporate sense — it is an independent open-source project with NVIDIA contributions.
verdicts.note: Open GitHub issues #3294 and #2577 explicitly document the sm_120 cubin gap as of 2026. The Apache-2.0 license is confirmed.

verdicts.fixes: The version description 'continuously updated; works on RTX 5090 with torch 2.9.0+cu128' is outdated. PyPI vllm latest is 0.22.0 (May 29, 2026) and ships with torch 2.11 (not 2.9). CUDA 12.8 is still the correct baseline for Blackwell support, but torch 2.9 reference is stale. The 'torch 2.9.0+cu128' description reflects an older community workaround from early 2026, not the current release baseline. NVIDIA's CUDA 13.1.1 is the basis for the latest NVIDIA vLLM release (26.02). Blackwell support confirmed working. Linux-only platform confirmed. Apache-2.0 license confirmed.
verdicts.note: FA4 is now the default attention backend on Blackwell SM100/SM103 in vLLM; SM120 consumer Blackwell still uses FA2-via-Triton. Safetensors/GPTQ/AWQ/FP8 model format claims confirmed.

verdicts.fixes: blackwell_ready: true is MISLEADING. Machete uses Hopper-specific wgmma PTX instructions (SM90a) that do not carry forward to Blackwell SM100+. W4A8 via Machete has NO registered kernel covering SM100 for that scheme — this is an active vLLM issue (#35439). Marlin W4A16 works on Blackwell via more portable instruction paths, but this is kernel-specific. The claim 'Blackwell_ready: true' should be qualified: Marlin W4A16 works on Blackwell; Machete W4A8 does NOT work on Blackwell as of 2026. The 'Marlin extended to Turing+ in Apr 2026' claim is plausible. The developer attribution mixing IST-Austria/Neural Magic/Red Hat is accurate for the provenance but the shipped code in vLLM is Apache-2.0. The model_formats claim (GPTQ, AWQ, compressed-tensors w4a16/w8a16) is correct for supported cases.
verdicts.note: The deepwiki source and RedHat Machete article both confirm the Hopper-specific instruction dependency. vLLM issue #35439 explicitly documents the SM100 gap for W4A8.

verdicts.fixes: Latest version is 0.0.35 (released February 20, 2026), NOT 0.0.32 as claimed. The researcher's latest_version field is three minor releases behind. The blackwell_ready: false claim is confirmed correct for official prebuilt PyPI wheels — as of 0.0.35, prebuilt wheels still do not target sm_120 (only up to sm_89/Ada Lovelace). The cutlass-blackwell FMHA operators are absent in the official wheels as of late April 2026 per community reports. Community sm_120 builds exist (xiangxin2025cn fork) but are not official. proposed_additions.name: ThunderKittens 2.0 (HazyResearch/Stanford)
proposed_additions.why: A CUDA DSL for writing attention and GEMM kernels, released v2.0 on January 11 2026 with full Blackwell (SM100/SM110) support, MXFP8/NVFP4 precision, and BF16/FP8 attention forward+backward running at near-cuDNN speeds on B200. Apache-licensed (per GitHub), open-source, and Together AI has already shipped production kernels on top of it — it is a first-class GPU kernel engine in this lane that the researcher skipped entirely.

proposed_additions.name: NATTEN (Neighborhood Attention)
proposed_additions.why: MIT-licensed sparse/neighborhood attention library (SHI-Labs) with Hopper and Blackwell (SM100) FMHA kernels achieving 1.3 petaFLOPs/s FP16 on B200, covering sliding-window and multi-dimensional sparse attention patterns that FlashAttention and cuDNN SDPA do not. Published at ICLR 2025 and extended via arXiv 2504.16922 (April 2025). A relevant omission for any workload using local or windowed attention (e.g., video models, Swin-style architectures).

proposed_additions.name: TensorRT-LLM FusedMHCA / trtllm-gen FMHA backend (NVIDIA)
proposed_additions.why: NVIDIA's production inference library ships its own fused multi-head attention (FMHA) kernels as precompiled cubins used by both TensorRT-LLM and (via flashinfer-cubin) FlashInfer. It is the ground-truth source of datacenter-Blackwell (SM100a/SM103a) cubin availability and the root cause of the sm_120 consumer-Blackwell gaps documented in FlashInfer and vLLM. Apache-2.0 licensed, Linux-only, and directly relevant to understanding which attention backends are actually deployable on Blackwell.

verify.receipt: Adversarial verification was performed by fetching or searching live sources for all 10 engines on 2026-06-02. Key catches: (1) xFormers version is 0.0.35 (Feb 2026), not 0.0.32 — three releases behind. (2) FlashAttention 4 version is beta15 (May 27 2026), not beta4 — ten beta releases behind, and the blackwell_ready:false flag is partially wrong since FA4 beta6+ added SM120 forward/backward code paths, though those paths use SM80-style MMA rather than FA4's TMEM-accelerated fast path. (3) triton-windows developer attribution is stale — the woct0rdho repo was archived Feb 18 2026 and development moved to triton-lang/triton-windows. (4) FlashInfer's blackwell_ready:true is overstated: AOT wheels ship zero sm_120/sm_121 cubins (documented in issue #3294), making it unreliable on consumer Blackwell RTX 5090. (5) Marlin/Machete blackwell_ready:true is misleading — Machete is Hopper-specific (SM90a wgmma PTX); only Marlin W4A16 paths work portably on Blackwell. (6) SageAttention version 2.2.0 is a GitHub tag; the pip package sageattention peaks at 1.0.6. (7) vLLM's torch 2.9.0 reference is stale; current release (0.22.0, May 2026) ships with torch 2.11. Three strong omissions were identified: ThunderKittens 2.0 (Blackwell CUDA DSL with production adoption), NATTEN (sparse/neighborhood attention with Blackwell FMHA kernels), and TensorRT-LLM's trtllm-gen FMHA backend (the actual source of datacenter-Blackwell cubins consumed by FlashInfer and vLLM).

research.domain: Training & fine-tuning engines (full fine-tune, LoRA/QLoRA, RLHF/DPO/GRPO) — frameworks that train AI models
research.notes:
DECISIVE AXIS for this rig = native-Windows viability without WSL2 + single-GPU LoRA/QLoRA fit on 32 GB VRAM. The big 2026 inversion: bitsandbytes now ships OFFICIAL prebuilt Windows x86-64 wheels that include sm_120 (Blackwell) targets for CUDA 12.8/12.9/13.0 (per the HF install matrix). That means 4-bit QLoRA on a 5090 runs on native Windows via plain `pip install bitsandbytes` — the old "you must use WSL2 for QLoRA" advice is dead. Second inversion: PyTorch's stable build matrix moved cu128 -> cu130 (CUDA 13.0 is the default; cu126 kept for old drivers; cu128 removed as of 2.12.0). sm_120 has been in stable PyTorch since 2.7, so a 5090 is a first-class PyTorch citizen now — `pip install torch --index-url.../whl/cu130` just works on Windows. Third: FSDP1 is deprecated (FSDP2 is the path), and torchtune development has wound down (legacy). WHAT TO ACTUALLY INSTALL for this lane (in order):
1. **Unsloth** — the primary daily driver for LLM LoRA/QLoRA. Single-GPU optimized, 2x faster + ~70% less VRAM via custom Triton kernels, Apache-2.0 core. On a 5090 you can QLoRA a 14B comfortably in VRAM and reach ~30-70B by spilling the paged AdamW optimizer state into the 64 GB system RAM. CAVEAT: Unsloth's smoothest install path still assumes Linux/WSL2 (its vLLM/xformers build notes target WSL2); native-Windows works but is the rougher road. For a Windows-only rig, run Unsloth inside WSL2 (Ubuntu) where the bitsandbytes+xformers+triton stack is frictionless.
2. **Hugging Face TRL v1.0 + PEFT (+ Liger-Kernel)** — the flexible, fully-Windows-native fallback and the right tool for DPO/GRPO/reward-modeling. TRL v1.0 absorbed PEFT + data-packing + an Unsloth fast path; PEFT gives LoRA/QLoRA; Liger-Kernel (BSD-2, drop-in `use_liger_kernel=True`) cuts another ~60% memory + ~20% throughput via fused Triton kernels. This whole stack is pure-Python over PyTorch+bitsandbytes, so it runs on NATIVE Windows today with the new sm_120 wheels — no WSL2 required.
3. **kohya_ss / sd-scripts** — NOT an LLM tool, but THE engine for the studio's actual headline need: SDXL/Flux style-LoRA training. It's the Windows-native standard for diffusion LoRA, and a 5090's 32 GB makes SDXL LoRA trivial and Flux LoRA (with FP8) comfortable. This is the one that ties directly to style-dataset-lab output. SKIP for this rig: DeepSpeed/Megatron-Core/NeMo are multi-GPU/datacenter engines — ZeRO-3 NVMe-offload can technically squeeze a big full-finetune onto one card, but on Windows DeepSpeed is painful (no official Windows wheels; inference-only adapter at best) and the juice isn't worth it on a single GPU; prefer Unsloth/PEFT. Axolotl and LLaMA-Factory are excellent YAML-driven orchestrators but are Linux/WSL2-first; reach for them (inside WSL2) only when you want config-file reproducibility or a recipe zoo, not as the default. torchtune is now legacy — don't start new work on it. Bottom line: for a single Windows 5090, the answer is Unsloth (in WSL2) for fast LLM LoRA + TRL/PEFT/Liger (native Windows) for everything flexible/RLHF + kohya_ss for the diffusion style-LoRA work that is the studio's real payload.

Key knobs: `load_in_4bit=True`, `use_gradient_checkpointing='unsloth'`, `max_seq_length`, LoRA rank/alpha.

extras.name: Native-Windows QLoRA on the 5090 (no WSL2) — TRL + PEFT + bitsandbytes + Liger
extras.note: THE big unlock. bitsandbytes now ships prebuilt Windows x86-64 wheels that include sm_120 (Blackwell) for CUDA 12.8/12.9/13.0 — so plain `pip install bitsandbytes` gives working 4-bit QLoRA on native Windows. Stack: `pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130` (or cu126 if on an older driver; cu128 was removed from the matrix), then `pip install transformers trl peft bitsandbytes accelerate liger-kernel`. In code: load with BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type='nf4', bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16, bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True); SFTConfig(packing=True, gradient_checkpointing=True, optim='paged_adamw_8bit', bf16=True); pass use_liger_kernel=True. Paged 8-bit AdamW spills optimizer state into the 64 GB system RAM so a 14B QLoRA fits comfortably in 32 GB VRAM.

extras.name: Unsloth on the 5090 (run inside WSL2 Ubuntu for the smooth path)
extras.note: Blackwell install per Unsloth docs: `uv pip install -U vllm --torch-backend=cu128` (forces cu128 torch so vLLM doesn't pull a cu126 build) then `uv pip install unsloth unsloth_zoo bitsandbytes`. If xformers fails to compile under WSL2, raise the WSL2 memory ceiling to >=16 GB in.wslconfig. In code: FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(model, load_in_4bit=True, max_seq_length=...); FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(..., use_gradient_checkpointing='unsloth'). The 'unsloth' checkpointing mode is the one that buys the big VRAM cut and lets 30-70B QLoRA fit by paging weights + optimizer into the 64 GB RAM. Native Windows works but WSL2 is the documented, frictionless route.

extras.name: SDXL / Flux style-LoRA on the 5090 with kohya_ss (native Windows)
extras.note: Pin a torch build with sm_120 support (cu128/cu130) — early 5090 users hit slow s/it and xformers CUDA errors on stale stacks. Use --mixed_precision bf16 and SDPA (or an sm_120-aware xformers). FP8: --fp8_base drops SDXL footprint ~29->22 GB; the fused backward pass takes SDXL to ~10 GB at bf16, so on 32 GB you can push higher LoRA/LoKr ranks, larger batch, or cached latents (--cache_latents). This is the engine that consumes style-dataset-lab training packages and produces the studio's style diffusion LoRAs.

extras.name: Single-GPU full-finetune that won't fit in 32 GB — FSDP2 CPUOffload into 64 GB RAM
extras.note: Last-resort path when you need a FULL (not LoRA) finetune of a model just over 32 GB. FSDP2 with CPUOffload pushes params + optimizer state into the 64 GB system RAM; combine with activation checkpointing and bf16. FSDP1 is deprecated — use the FSDP2 API (fully_shard). Expect it to be PCIe/CPU-bandwidth-bound and slow on one GPU; for most studio needs QLoRA in Unsloth/PEFT is the better answer. Prefer DeepSpeed ZeRO-Infinity NVMe-offload only inside WSL2 and only if FSDP2 CPUOffload still OOMs.

extras.name: Driver / CUDA toolchain baseline for sm_120 on Windows
extras.note: sm_120 (RTX 5090) has been in stable PyTorch since 2.7; current stable is 2.12.0 (2026-05-13). Install rule of thumb on Windows: recent NVIDIA Game-Ready/Studio driver (CUDA 13.x capable) + the cu130 torch wheel. If a dependency hasn't shipped sm_120 yet you'll see 'no kernel image is available for execution on the device' — fix by upgrading that dep or compiling it (bitsandbytes/xformers) against CUDA 12.8+; for bitsandbytes specifically the prebuilt Windows wheel already covers sm_120, so usually no source build needed.

extras.name: Liger-Kernel (drop-in fused Triton kernels)
extras.note: BSD-2-Clause, v0.8.0 (2026-04-30). Enable under TRL/HF Trainer with use_liger_kernel=True, or via flags in Axolotl/LLaMA-Factory. ~20% throughput + ~60% memory for free; fused-linear-cross-entropy and DPO/ORPO/CPO/SimPO/KTO loss kernels claim up to 80% memory savings. Always turn it on. Blackwell support rides on your Triton build being sm_120-aware.

extras.name: kohya_ss GUI (bmaltais) — front-end over sd-scripts

verify.receipt: Verified all 11 engines against live PyPI pages, GitHub release pages, official documentation, and NVIDIA NGC catalog as of 2026-06-02. Key catches: TRL latest_version is v1.5.1 (not v1.0, which is four minor versions stale); kohya sd-scripts latest is v0.10.5 (not ~v0.9.x, which was superseded by an entire major minor version); Megatron-Core latest is v0.17.1 (not v0.16.1, released May 28 2026); LLaMA-Factory latest is v0.9.5 (not v0.9.4, released May 30 2026). research.domain: Diffusion inference engines & accelerators (image/video) — the engine/accelerator layer beneath ComfyUI workflows, filtered for a single RTX 5090 / Blackwell sm_120 / Windows 11 / 32 GB VRAM + 64 GB RAM local game-studio rig
research.notes: DECISIVE AXIS for this rig: Windows-native Blackwell (sm_120) support + VRAM economics on a single 32 GB card. Most diffusion accelerators are Linux-first; the ones that actually pay off here are the ComfyUI-native ones plus a couple of permissively-licensed kernel/quant libs. WHAT CHANGED (inverts old advice): (1) ComfyUI's official Windows portable now ships its OWN pinned PyTorch build on CUDA 13.0 + Python 3.13 that runs on Blackwell out of the box — this is exactly why the rig rule says "do NOT hand-install torch nightly." If you install via portable, Comfy pins torch for you; the lingering "you still need nightly" guides on the web apply to people hand-building a venv (stable PyTorch 2.7 added sm_120 cu128 wheels but Windows packaging + FlashAttention lagged through the 2.8/2.9 line — sources: pytorch/pytorch#164342). (2) NEVER pip install xformers on a Blackwell nightly/portable env — it silently corrupts the install; use SageAttention instead (Comfy-Org discussion #11583). (3) Nunchaku + NVFP4 is now the headline single-GPU win: ~3x over BF16 with near-16-bit quality and ~3.6x VRAM cut on FLUX, native on the 5090's FP4 tensor cores (hanlab/MIT blog; Nunchaku v1.2.x, Apache-2.0). (4) stable-fast is effectively retired — its author moved to Comfy-WaveSpeed (FBCache/TeaCache for ComfyUI); do not start new work on stable-fast. INSTALL THESE THREE for this lane: (1) ComfyUI (portable, GPL-3.0) as the runtime/engine — non-negotiable base. (2) Nunchaku (Apache-2.0) for 4-bit NVFP4 FLUX/Qwen-Image — the biggest speed+VRAM lever for a 32 GB card, and it frees VRAM headroom for LoRA stacks and ControlNets. (3) ComfyUI-GGUF (city96, Apache-2.0) for the heavy video/large models (Wan, large FLUX/Qwen) where you need RAM/CPU partial offload to spill past 32 GB VRAM into the 64 GB system RAM. Add SageAttention (permissive, but verify the exact kernel variant for commercial use) as the universal attention accelerator under all of them — ~30-35% sampling speedup, the sanctioned xformers replacement on Blackwell. Comfy-WaveSpeed (FBCache) is the near-zero-cost cache layer to stack on top for an extra ~1.5-2x on iterative work. SKIP / DEMOTE on this rig: xDiT and ParaAttention's context-parallel path are multi-GPU/datacenter tools — single 5090 gets only their cache/compile features, which ComfyUI already exposes more conveniently. TensorRT is real speed (FP4 on Blackwell) but Windows-on-5090 has had broken builds and a per-resolution engine-compile tax that fights an iterative studio workflow — situational, best for a fixed-resolution batch pipeline. OneDiff's best quantization is gated behind a paid Enterprise license — community build is fine but Nunchaku/GGUF cover the same ground freely. DeepCache is SD1.5/SDXL-UNet era; for modern DiT models (FLUX/Wan/Qwen) use FBCache/TeaCache instead.

engines.summary: Nunchaku is the single biggest speed+VRAM lever for a 32 GB Blackwell card. It runs SVDQuant 4-bit diffusion (absorbs activation outliers into a low-rank branch, so 4-bit quality stays near 16-bit) and on the RTX 5090 uses native NVFP4 tensor-core kernels for ~3x throughput and ~3.6x VRAM reduction on FLUX.1-dev — that freed headroom is what lets you stack LoRAs, ControlNets, and higher batch sizes on one card. Supports FLUX.1 (dev/schnell/Krea/Kontext/tools), Qwen-Image + Qwen-Image-Edit, SANA, Z-Image-Turbo, with native ComfyUI nodes and seamless LoRA as of v1.2.x (compatible with ComfyUI 0.7). On Blackwell prefer the NVFP4 checkpoints over INT4 for quality; NVFP4 paths want CUDA 12.8+/13. Gotcha: it's a quant-runtime, not a general engine — you load Nunchaku-format models, so coverage is limited to the families they've quantized (no SDXL UNet, no Wan video yet).

engines.summary: ComfyUI-GGUF is the VRAM-fit workhorse for this rig: it brings llama.cpp-style GGUF variable-bitrate quantization to native ComfyUI diffusion models, so heavy models that won't fit at 32 GB (large FLUX, Qwen-Image, and especially Wan video) run at Q8 down to Q4 with graceful degradation, and weights spill from VRAM into your 64 GB system RAM via partial offload. Use the 'Unet Loader (GGUF)' (place.gguf in models/unet) and the GGUF CLIPLoader nodes to also quantize the T5 text encoder, which alone reclaims several GB. This is the right tool precisely where Nunchaku doesn't reach — video models and families nobody has SVDQuant-packed. Gotcha: Wan 2.x contains 5D tensors that exceed GGUF dims and must be split out via fix_5d_tensors.py during conversion; and GGUF is a fit/offload play, not a throughput play (it can be slower than fp8 when fully VRAM-resident).

engines.summary: Comfy-WaveSpeed is the spiritual successor to the now-retired stable-fast (same author) and the practical home of dynamic caching in ComfyUI. Its 'Apply First Block Cache' node uses the first transformer block's residual as a change indicator: when consecutive residuals barely differ, it reuses the prior output and skips the remaining blocks, giving ~1.5-2x on iterative DiT models (FLUX, HunyuanVideo, Wan) at near-zero VRAM cost — it stacks cleanly on top of SageAttention and Nunchaku. Knobs: a residual_diff_threshold trades speed vs fidelity (higher = faster, more artifacts). This is the cheapest extra speed in the lane for a single 5090. Gotcha: it's WIP and some node combinations (e.g., certain Kijai HunyuanVideo nodes) are incompatible; caching can soften fine detail at aggressive thresholds, so tune per workflow. The multi-GPU context-parallel path (ParaAttention port) is not relevant on one card.

It runs on Blackwell wherever your PyTorch does. On Windows the gotcha is the same torch/sm_120 pinning as everything else, plus torch.compile on Windows is less battle-tested than on Linux (Triton-Windows required). For a ComfyUI-centric studio it's the secondary, scripting-and-training tool — not your primary inference path.

The catch makes it situational for an iterative studio: you pick Static (one resolution/batch, max speed) or Dynamic (a min/opt/max range, slightly slower) engines, and changing model, LoRA, or resolution means recompiling — a tax that fights exploratory art work. Best reserved for a locked-down, fixed-resolution batch pipeline (e.g., mass sprite re-renders at one size) rather than your daily-driver canvas. For most local diffusion, Nunchaku + SageAttention + FBCache deliver most of the speed with none of the recompile pain.

engines.speed_note: Training-free UNet feature caching: ~2.3x for SD1.5, ~4.1x for LDM. Exploits U-Net high-level feature redundancy across denoising steps — but it's a U-Net technique, not a DiT one.
engines.summary: DeepCache (CVPR 2024) is a training-free caching method that exploits temporal redundancy in U-Net diffusion: it reuses high-level features across adjacent denoising steps while cheaply refreshing low-level ones, giving ~2.3x on SD1.5 and big gains on LDM at tiny quality cost. It's Apache-2.0 and plug-and-play on Diffusers. The catch for 2026 is architectural: DeepCache is built around the U-Net skip structure, so it applies to SD1.5/SDXL/SVD — NOT the modern FLUX/Wan/Qwen-Image diffusion TRANSFORMERS this studio targets. For DiTs, First Block Cache / TeaCache (Comfy-WaveSpeed, ParaAttention) is the correct successor. Keep DeepCache only if you still run SDXL-era pipelines; for new work it's superseded.

extras.name: Clean Blackwell ComfyUI install on Windows (do NOT hand-install torch)
extras.note: Use the official Windows PORTABLE build — it ships its own pinned PyTorch on CUDA 13.0 + Python 3.13 that runs on sm_120 out of the box. Do NOT pip install torch nightly into it; let Comfy own the torch pin. NEVER run 'pip install xformers' in this env — it silently corrupts the Blackwell install. Verify GPU is seen: python_embeded\python.exe -c "import torch;print(torch.cuda.get_device_name(0), torch.version.cuda)" should print the 5090 + CUDA 13.x.

extras.name: SageAttention on the 5090 — version-pinned wheel + launch flag
extras.note: Install a prebuilt sm_120 SageAttention 2.2.x wheel that MATCHES your exact torch build (the wheels are pinned to a specific PyTorch nightly date / cu128; a mismatch throws DLL load errors). For portable: python_embeded\python.exe -m pip install <sageattention-...win_amd64.whl>. Then launch ComfyUI with --use-sage-attention for ~30-35% faster sampling. If the CUDA-kernel path is unstable on your card, the Triton-Windows fallback works (install triton-windows) but is slower. This is the sanctioned xformers replacement.

extras.name: Nunchaku NVFP4 FLUX/Qwen-Image on a 32 GB card
extras.note: Install the nunchaku wheel + the ComfyUI-nunchaku nodes; pull the NVFP4 (not INT4) checkpoints for FLUX.1-dev / Qwen-Image — on Blackwell NVFP4 is both faster and higher quality, ~3x over BF16 with ~3.6x less VRAM. NVFP4 paths want CUDA 12.8+/13 (comfy-kitchen). The freed VRAM is what lets you stack multiple LoRAs + ControlNets on one 5090. v1.2.x has native LoRA nodes and works with ComfyUI 0.7.

extras.name: GGUF partial offload to spill into 64 GB system RAM (Wan / large FLUX)
extras.note: For models that won't fit in 32 GB VRAM (Wan video, large FLUX/Qwen): place.gguf in ComfyUI/models/unet, use the 'Unet Loader (GGUF)' node, and pick Q8 (best quality) down to Q4 (smallest). Also quantize the T5 text encoder via the GGUF CLIPLoader nodes to reclaim several GB. ComfyUI/PyTorch will partial-offload to your 64 GB RAM when VRAM is exceeded. Wan 2.x 5D tensors must be split out with fix_5d_tensors.py during conversion.

extras.name: Stack First Block Cache (Comfy-WaveSpeed) for free ~2x
extras.note: Add the 'Apply First Block Cache' node after your model loader; tune residual_diff_threshold (higher = faster but more detail loss, start ~0.12 for FLUX). Composes cleanly on top of SageAttention + Nunchaku for compounding speedups on iterative DiT sampling. Some node combos (e.g. certain Kijai HunyuanVideo nodes) are incompatible — disable the cache there.

extras.name: Diffusers programmatic VRAM + Blackwell quant recipe
extras.note: For scripted pipelines / LoRA training: combine torchao NVFP4 (or MXFP8 for the quality 'sweet spot') quantization + torch.compile (needs triton-windows on Windows) for ~1.26-1.68x on Blackwell, and pipe.enable_group_offload(offload_type='leaf_level', use_stream=True) to spill modules into the 64 GB system RAM. FP8 layerwise casting (enable_layerwise_casting) roughly halves weight memory with minimal quality loss.

extras.name: triton-windows
extras.note: Required on Windows for torch.compile and as the SageAttention Triton fallback path. Pair with the portable torch build; this is what replaces xformers-style fused kernels on Blackwell.

extras.name: ComfyUI-Win-Blackwell (reference clean-install repo)
extras.note: An open-sourced, fully-documented Windows-native ComfyUI setup specifically for RTX 5090/5080/5070 (sm_120) with CUDA 13.0 — useful as a known-good reference when an install goes sideways, listing verified custom nodes and tested I2V pipelines.

extras.name: NVIDIA Model-Optimizer (TensorRT-LLM / diffusers FP4)
extras.note: NVIDIA's quantization toolkit for producing FP4/FP8 diffusion engines (the path behind TensorRT FP4 image gen on Blackwell). Use only if you commit to the fixed-resolution TensorRT route; otherwise Nunchaku covers 4-bit on this rig without the recompile tax.

extras.name: PyTorch sm_120 stable-support tracking issue
extras.note: Canonical tracker for when stable PyTorch fully covers sm_120 on Windows (FlashAttention etc.). Confirms 2.7 added cu128 sm_120 wheels but Windows packaging lagged through the 2.8/2.9 line — the reason the rig rule says lean on ComfyUI's pinned portable torch rather than rolling your own.

verify.receipt: Verification was conducted via 20+ web searches and direct page fetches against live GitHub repos, PyPI listings, official documentation, and news sources as of June 2, 2026. Key catches: (1) ComfyUI version numbering is wrong — the researcher conflated Desktop app versioning (v0.7.0 = ROCm Desktop, Jan 2026) with the core backend release series, which is now at v0.23.0 (June 1, 2026); (2) Nunchaku's developer org has migrated from nunchaku-tech to nunchaku-ai — the repo_url is stale; (3) SageAttention and OneDiff both had commercial_use marked 'conditional' without basis — SageAttention is straightforward Apache-2.0 (commercial: yes), while OneDiff's Apache-2.0 community tier is also unconditionally commercial (only the Enterprise quantization tier is paid); (4) OneDiff's blackwell_ready=true claim is unsubstantiated — the live repo lists no Blackwell GPU compatibility and has had no release since July 2024, making it 'superseded' in currency; (5) DeepCache's blackwell_ready=true is self-contradictory given it is explicitly a UNet-era wrapper with no DiT/FLUX support and no Blackwell documentation; (6) ComfyUI_TensorRT developer attribution mixed up comfyanonymous (individual, correct repo owner) with Comfy-Org (incorrect); (7) Diffusers 0.38.0 is a May 2026 release, not a '2025 cut' as the researcher parenthetically stated; (8) ParaAttention's Windows 'partial' support claim is unverified — all documented benchmarks target Linux GPU clusters. Three significant omissions were identified: stable-diffusion.cpp (the C/C++ GGUF inference engine, actively shipping in 2026), torchao (the actual upstream mechanism for Blackwell FP4/FP8 in most engines listed), and InvokeAI (Apache-2.0 commercial-grade alternative to GPL-3.0 ComfyUI).

research.domain: Foundational tensor runtimes, compilers, and cross-platform backends (the "what is underneath" lane) — the substrate every higher-level inference server / training framework is built on, filtered for a single RTX 5090 / Blackwell sm_120 / Windows 11 workstation.
research.notes: DECISIVE AXIS for this rig = "stable Blackwell wheels on Windows-native, today." On that axis the lane splits cleanly. INSTALL THESE THREE: (1) PyTorch (cu130 or cu126 build, NOT cu128) — it is the floor everything else stands on; diffusion/ComfyUI, LoRA training (PEFT/Diffusers), and most local tooling are PyTorch. Blackwell has been stable on Windows since 2.7.0 (Apr 2026); the current 2.12.0 (May 2026) DROPPED cu128 from the build matrix, so the years-old "pip install... --index-url.../cu128" advice now installs nothing — use cu130 (CUDA 13) as default, cu126 only for old drivers. This is the single biggest recently-inverted fact in the lane. (2) ggml / llama.cpp — the offload king. Windows CUDA prebuilts ship every few days (b9484 carries CUDA 12.4 + 13.3 DLL bundles), no compile needed, and GGUF partial offload (-ngl plus --n-cpu-moe / tensor-split) is exactly what turns 64 GB system RAM into "models a bit over 32 GB VRAM still run." This is the local-LLM-delegation workhorse. (3) TensorRT-RTX — the *consumer-RTX* TensorRT (NOT datacenter TensorRT, NOT TRT-LLM which is WSL2-only on GeForce). <200 MB, native Windows pip wheel (pip install tensorrt-rtx), JIT engine build so no fragile per-GPU AOT step, covers Turing→Blackwell CC 10.0. Reach for it when a frozen ONNX/diffusion model needs the last 1.5-2x of latency. SECONDARY: ONNX Runtime is worth having as the portable glue layer (CUDA EP for NVIDIA speed, or the new WinML/DirectML path for vendor-neutral Windows GPU/NPU) and the standard exchange format; Triton matters but you get it for free bundled inside PyTorch on Windows — you rarely install it standalone. AVOID FOR THIS RIG (record as reference only): JAX/XLA is WSL2-only on Windows (native GPU pip silently fails) and is a research/TPU stack, not a studio inference tool; OpenVINO is Intel-silicon-first (great for the Core Ultra NPU/iGPU, irrelevant to the 5090); Apache TVM is a research compiler with no Blackwell story and Windows-build friction; MLX is Apple-Silicon-only (no Mac here) — pure cross-platform reference. WHAT CHANGED RECENTLY (2026): stable Blackwell on Windows is now boring/solved at the PyTorch layer (2.7→2.12), the CUDA-13 cutover is live and breaks copy-pasted cu128 commands, official Triton finally owns Windows support (community fork archived Feb 2026), and WSL3 (announced Build 2026) promises near-native GPU passthrough — which will eventually make JAX viable on this box, but not yet.

engines.summary: The C/C++ tensor library (ggml) + LLM runtime (llama.cpp) that is the single best local-LLM-delegation engine for this rig. It ships rolling Windows prebuilt binaries with CUDA bundles (current b9484 carries CUDA 12.4 and CUDA 13.3 DLL packs) — unzip and run, no toolchain or WSL2 required, and Blackwell works via the CUDA backend. The decisive feature for a 32 GB-VRAM + 64 GB-RAM box is partial offload: -ngl/--n-gpu-layers puts as many layers on the 5090 as fit, the rest spill to system RAM, and for MoE models --n-cpu-moe / --override-tensor keeps expert tensors on CPU so a model far larger than 32 GB still runs. Other key knobs: --flash-attn, --cache-type-k/-v q8_0 (KV-cache quant to stretch context), --ctx-size, and --tensor-split for multi-GPU. Use it for the 'ollama-intern' style bulk-analysis delegation and any local-first chat/agent that must not burn cloud tokens; it powers Ollama and LM Studio underneath.

engines.summary: The consumer-RTX-targeted TensorRT — a compact (<200 MB) drop-in inference compiler for NVIDIA RTX GPUs from Turing (7.5) through Blackwell (compute capability 10.0), and the *right* TensorRT for this rig (datacenter TensorRT and TRT-LLM are heavier and TRT-LLM on GeForce is WSL2-only). It installs as a native Windows pip wheel (pip install tensorrt-rtx; append -cu12 or -cu13 to pick the CUDA variant, default CUDA 13.x), takes an ONNX model and JIT-builds an optimized engine at load time so you avoid the brittle ahead-of-time per-GPU plan files of classic TensorRT. Reach for it when a model is frozen (a production diffusion UNet/VAE, an upscaler, a vision model) and you want the last 1.5-3x of latency and FP8/FP4 Blackwell tensor-core throughput that eager PyTorch leaves on the table. Gotchas: NVIDIA-only and proprietary; it optimizes a static graph, so it's for inference of fixed shapes/models, not flexible training; recent releases note Blackwell-specific Compute-in-Graphics (CiG) fixes.

engines.summary: Microsoft's cross-platform ONNX inference (and limited training) runtime — the portable glue layer and standard exchange format of the lane. On this Windows+5090 rig you have two good lanes: the CUDA Execution Provider (or chain the TensorRT EP) for full NVIDIA performance, or DirectML/WinML for a vendor-neutral DX12 path that needs no CUDA install and also reaches the Intel Core Ultra iGPU/NPU. 1.26.0 (May 2026) raised the CUDA floor to 12.0 (CUDA 11.x dropped) and publishes separate cuda12/cuda13 GPU packages, and it has been built successfully for Blackwell. engines.language: Python DSL → MLIR → PTX/CUDA (and AMD/Intel backends)
engines.commercial_notes: MIT — permissive. The Windows forks were also MIT/community; using the bundled-with-PyTorch Triton on Windows carries no extra license burden.

engines.speed_note: It IS the speed: TorchInductor emits Triton kernels, so most of torch.compile's speedup on Blackwell is Triton. Hand-written Triton kernels (fused attention, custom GEMM) can beat library defaults but are an engineering project.
engines.summary: The Python-embedded GPU-kernel language and MLIR-based compiler that underpins TorchInductor — when torch.compile speeds up your model on the 5090, Triton is generating the fused CUDA kernels. Blackwell needs Triton >= 3.3; the current official line is 3.7.0 (and Triton 3.6 pairs with PyTorch >= 2.10). The Windows reality is the nuance: the official triton-lang/triton is Linux-only, Windows support lived in the community woct0rdho/triton-windows fork (v3.6.0, now ARCHIVED as of Feb 2026) and has been folded into the official triton-lang/triton-windows — but in practice you get a working Triton automatically when you install the PyTorch Windows wheel, so you rarely pip-install it standalone. Reach for hand-written Triton only when you have a specific hot kernel (a custom attention or quant-dequant fusion) that the autotuner doesn't nail; otherwise let torch.compile use it for you. Gotcha on Blackwell+Windows: occasional 'sm_120 is not defined for option gpu-name' errors come from a mismatched Triton/CUDA/PyTorch trio — keep all three on the same generation (PyTorch >= 2.10, recent Triton, CUDA 12.8+).

CUDA 12.8 was the FIRST toolkit to support Blackwell across the whole tool/library/compiler suite and introduced Compute-in-Graphics (CiG) on Windows x64 for Blackwell GeForce; the line has since moved to CUDA 13.x (which PyTorch 2.12 adopts as default, dropping the older 12.8 wheels). Native Windows is fully supported; WSL2 is only needed for the Linux-first frameworks (JAX, TRT-LLM) that sit above it.
